notes.meaning: Manasseh became king as a boy of twelve. He ruled for fifty-five years, longer than any other king of Judah. Being so young, he may have been easily led astray, though he surely had a godly upbringing. One commentary sees the long reign as God's mercy, giving him time to repent.

Manasseh turned his back on the good example and training of his father Hezekiah. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations God had driven out of the land. Parents can give their children many good things, but they cannot give them God's grace.

Manasseh undid his father's reforms. He rebuilt the "high places," local hilltop shrines. He set up altars to Baal and poles for the goddess Asherah, and he worshiped the sun, moon and stars. Star worship was linked with Assyria, Babylon and astrology. Even good reforms do not last on their own.

Manasseh went further and put pagan altars inside God's own temple, in both its courtyards. This was the very house where God had promised His Name would stay forever. He made the holy place unclean with idol worship. His sins kept growing, each one worse than the last.

Manasseh burned his own sons as offerings to the pagan god Moloch in the Valley of Hinnom. He turned to sorcery and fortune-telling and let spirit-mediums guide him instead of God. One commentary notes that sin clouds the mind as well as spoiling the soul. All this stirred God to anger.

Worst of all, Manasseh set up a carved idol in the temple itself. It was probably an image of the goddess Asherah. God had chosen this house and city for His Name. He had promised Israel they would keep the land, if they obeyed the law He gave through Moses. Manasseh treated that choice and promise with contempt.

The king did not sin alone. He led the whole nation astray, until they did worse than the pagans God had driven out. The people's turning to God under Hezekiah had been shallow, so they slid back quickly. One sinful leader can do a world of harm.

God spoke to Manasseh and the people through His prophets, but they would not listen. Their hearts were not moved to believe and turn back. Even so, God's warning was a mercy. He still waited to be gracious when He could have judged them at once.

Because they would not listen, God sent the Assyrian army. This was probably under King Esarhaddon. The "hook" pictures Manasseh being led like a wild animal with a ring through its nose, and he was bound in double bronze chains. He was taken to Babylon, which was then under Assyrian rule. Assyrian records name "Manasseh of Judah" among the kings who submitted to Esarhaddon.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some nineteenth-century critics argued that the story of Manasseh's captivity and conversion was made up. Other scholars defended it as history, pointing to Assyrian records.

notes.meaning: In his trouble, Manasseh did not sin more, as King Ahaz had done. Instead he humbled himself and prayed to the God of his fathers. God heard him and brought him home to his throne. Hard times taught him what good times had not: the LORD alone is God. His story shows that no sinner is too far gone to be forgiven, because God's mercy is not earned.

Back home, Manasseh strengthened Jerusalem. He built up a high outer wall and put army commanders in Judah's fortified towns. His sin had left the city exposed. Now that he had turned back to God, he cared about protecting his people and guarding against another surprise attack.

Manasseh took the foreign gods, the idol and the pagan altars out of the temple and the city, and threw them outside. Each thing removed matches something he had set up earlier, so this was a deliberate turnaround. His changed actions showed that his repentance was real. Yet he threw the idols out rather than destroying them.

Manasseh repaired God's altar. He brought peace offerings to seek God's favor and thank offerings to praise Him for rescuing him. Once he had ordered idol worship, but now he ordered Judah to serve the LORD. True repentance tries to undo the harm we have done to others.

The people stopped worshiping false gods, but they kept sacrificing at the hilltop shrines, now to the LORD. This was not idol worship as such, but it was not the way God had commanded. Manasseh could not undo all the damage he had done. It is easy to lead people into sin and hard to bring them back.

The writer points to other records of Manasseh's reign. These were the royal records of Judah, here called "Israel," and the writings of the seers, or "Hozai." They held his prayer, the prophets' warnings, and a list of his sins. His prayer is mentioned twice, so later generations would praise God for welcoming back those who return. The prayer's actual words have not come down to us. The later "Prayer of Manasseh" found in the Apocrypha was written in Greek and is probably not his own words, though it has many good thoughts.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The official Latin Bible of the Catholic Church printed the Prayer of Manasseh in an appendix rather than as part of Scripture.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: For the Orthodox, the Prayer of Manasseh is part of the Bible. It is used in the evening service called Great Compline.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars usually see the Prayer of Manasseh as a Greek-speaking Jewish writer's attempt to recreate the prayer mentioned here.

notes.meaning: Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his palace, not in the royal tombs. Because of his great sins, he did not receive the honor his father had. People who repent may find peace with God sooner than they win back their good name. Some suggest his turnaround helps explain why the exile did not come in his day.
Amon, Manasseh's son, became king at twenty-two and reigned only two years. Unlike his father, he could not blame youth for his choices. He was a grown man who chose evil on purpose.

Amon copied his father's sins but not his repentance. He brought back the very idols Manasseh had thrown out but not destroyed, and his guilt only grew. It is not so much sin as refusing to repent of it that ruins people. Manasseh's story is in the Bible so old sinners will not despair. Amon's story is beside it so young people will not put off turning to God.

Amon's own servants plotted against him and killed him in his palace. We are not told why. Some suggest a power struggle over Judah's ties to Assyria. He had rebelled against God, and now his servants rebelled against him. God was just in this, but the plotters were still wicked.

The people of the land did not accept the murder. They rightly put the traitors to death and made Amon's young son Josiah king. After many years of wicked kings, this was a hopeful sign. Josiah would become one of Judah's best kings.
